extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and other Office personnel (secondary: patent applicants and practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for Office personnel on establishing and articulating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (pre-AIA 103(a) where applicable), including the Graham factual inquiries, search scope, analogous art, rationales for obviousness, and consideration of applicant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying factual inquiries enunciated in Graham v. John Deere Co.: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Graham factors, including secondary considerations when present, are the controlling inquiries in any obviousness analysis. Each case must be decided on its own facts; the sequence of questions may be reordered, but the factors define the inquiry. (Citations: Graham; KSR.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification including the claims. The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.' Once scope is determined, decide what to search for (claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed) and where to search (see MPEP §904–§904.03). Prior art can be within the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed by the inventor (see analogous art discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art by interpreting claim language and considering the invention and prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires claim interpretation (see MPEP §2111) and comparison with references. The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness; examiners must explain why differences would or would not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider may include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC). Every factor may not be present; one or more may predominate. Office personnel may rely on their own technical expertise to describe the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) relevant to obviousness may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be included in the specification at filing or provided timely during prosecution; weight is case-by-case. Presentation of such evidence is not dispositive, but Office personnel must evaluate it and articulate how it affects the obviousness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel must articulate factual findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When making an obviousness rejection, Office personnel must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of applied references and must explain the rationale(s) supporting the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notification of reasons for rejection. Findings should include, where appropriate, how a person of ordinary skill would have understood prior art teachings. Rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (In re Kahn; KSR). Clear findings and rationales facilitate prompt resolution and proper traversal by applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search should seek references that provide such teachings or suggestions if they exist. See MPEP §904 and §904.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search / analogous art consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: For 35 U.S.C. 103 purposes, prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem; examiners must determine what references are analogous art and where to search accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference may be analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (Bigio). Examiner may need to explain their understanding of the problem and factual reasons why a prior art reference would have commended itself to an inventor. Patent classification and cross-references provide some evidence but similarities/differences in structure and function carry greater weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight / content determined at time invention made
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art must be determined as of the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmaker must cast the mind back to what a person skilled in the art would have known at the time of invention; see MPEP §2145 and cited case law. Rebuttal arguments asserting hindsight must be considered and addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary rationales to support 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: List of illustrative rationales that may be used to support a conclusion of obviousness (not exclusive): (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' selecting from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in same or different field; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art leading one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is a valid rationale among others; KSR cautioned against rigid application but recognized TSM as capturing a helpful insight. The list is exemplary, not exhaustive. Office personnel should consider these and any other valid rationales, and must clearly articulate why claimed invention would have been obvious under the chosen rationale(s). See MPEP §2143 and §2144 et seq. for examples and further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSM (teaching-suggestion-motivation) rationale use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Graham inquiries reveal that an obviousness rejection may be made using TSM rationale, then such a rejection should be made, though not applied rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized TSM as one of a number of valid rationales and that there is no necessary inconsistency between TSM and Graham analysis. Examiners may rely on TSM but should also consider other rationales and must articulate the motivation or rationale supporting a combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for reasoned applicant reply (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When replying to an Office action, the applicant must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse to factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office erred substantively. Mere statements that the Office has not established a prima facie case, or unsupported assertions that reliance on common knowledge is improper, are insufficient. Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next action final per MPEP §706.07(a) if applicant's reply is not substantively adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including secondary considerations and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may show, for example: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (technological difficulties); (B) elements in combination do not merely perform their separate functions; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Examiners should reconsider the entire record in view of rebuttal evidence (In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly). Follow MPEP §706.07(a) in deciding finality and see MPEP §716–716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness regardless of statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on particular 102 categories depending on reference type and dates. For example, obviousness over a U.S. patent issued more than one year before filing may be a statutory bar as if anticipated under pre-AIA 102(b). Where applicable, applicants may overcome some references by swearing behind publication dates via affidavits/declarations (see MPEP §901–§901.06(d); §2121–§2129; §2151–§2155).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden of proof to show disqualification of certain prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wish to avail themselves of 103(c) benefits bear the burden of establishing common ownership or joint research agreement conditions for disqualifying certain prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish joint research agreement benefits, applicant must show: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on/before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose names of parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art test and how to support an analogous-art determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is analogous art if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (Bigio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applying the 'reasonably pertinent' prong, examiners should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support that the prior art is pertinent. The question often turns on how the problem is perceived; examiners must explain why an inventor would have looked to the reference. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem should be evaluated against the specification's teachings. Similarities and differences in structure and function of inventions carry significant weight in analogy determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities/differences in structure and function for analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a reference is reasonably pertinent (analogous), weigh similarities and differences in structure and function between the reference and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and search cross-references provide some evidence, but courts have found structural and functional comparisons to carry far greater weight (In re Ellis). Exemplar case law across chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts illustrates application of analogy tests.
